newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish politics embroiled in scandal.
newsitem.headline: Turkish politics embroiled in scandal.

text.p: A government MP on Thursday faced possible prosecution in a security scandal that is drawing Turkey's politicians deeper into a twilight world of gangsters, mystery murders and heroin trafficking.
Justice ministry officials said a prosecutor had asked in a report for legal steps to be taken to lift deputy Mehmet Agar's parliamentary immunity from legal censure.
"This report has reached our criminal affairs department. It is being studied," a ministry oficial told Reuters.

Agar, who quit as interior minister in November over the scandal, was accused this week of having signed a false police identity document for a fugitive gangster who was allegedly used by officials to kill Turkey's political opponents.
President Suleyman Demirel, who usually stays clear of day-to-day politics, has put his weight behind calls for five weeks of allegations to be cleared up.
"This is an important matter. It has to be brought to light. It has to go as far is it goes," he told Turkish television on Wednesday in a rare interview that was devoted to the scandal.

The media and opposition has alleged that leading officials directed hit squads to kill Kurdish rebel sympathisers and business rivals. More than 1,300 people have died since 1992 in unsolved political killings, human right activists say.
The scandal broke on November 3 when a car carrying a government MP who heads an anti-guerrilla Kurdish militia, a wanted gangster and a leading policeman crashed.
It has pushed problems like annual inflation of more than 80 percent, faltering revenue-raising plans and worsening relations with Europe almost off the political map.
Demirel said he feared the whole establishment could be tainted by the affair. "If the perpetrators are not found the state will get the blame. I am also uneasy about (the mystery killings)."
He said main opposition leader Mesut Yilmaz had given him names of "people in high places" involved in the scandal.

Demirel met Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan on Thursday evening for talks on Yilmaz's accusations that a network of up to 120 people directed by senior policemen are involved in murders, extortion and drug smuggling.

"Whatever is necessary will be brought out into the open. The state is legal state. If there is within the state, a person or group acting against the law, none of us can accept this," Erbakan said after the meeting.
Erbakan's coalition partner Tansu Ciller, linked by the media to the scandal, said the atmosphere of suspicion had dented public faith in the system.
"Turkey has been put under a cloud, from the office of the president to the police force and parliament," Foreign Minister Ciller told a meeting of her True Path Party.

Western diplomats say Ciller has lost much of her credibility for a speech she made last month in which she praised convicted heroin smuggler Abdullah Catli, who died in the crash, and suggested he had done political dirty work for the security apparatus.
Although Catli had been sought for murder for 18 years, a police identity document and a passport of a kind only issued to top officials were recovered in the car.
